q: Why is pEc45-2020-33kb non-transferable under standard conjugation conditions when the same IncX4/mcr-1 backbone is highly transmissible in the near-identical Chinese/European plasmids (KX711707, CP017246, MK940857) it shares >99.7% weighted identity with, and is this due to (a) loss/mutation of oriT that this replication has not yet localized, (b) trans-inhibition by the co-resident 254 kb IncH + 190 kb IncF plasmids (Szmolka's own 'conjugation competition' speculation), or (c) a strain-level regulatory silencing of T4SS that would not appear in the sequence alone?
basis: Szmolka et al. Discussion §3 explicitly flag this as unexpected and unresolved ('the oriT was not detectable ... we speculate a potential conjugation competition ... warrants further investigation'). Our BLAST rerun (evidence/blast_incx4_v2_summary.json) confirms the backbone including the virD4-taxC T4SS locus is essentially intact (>99.7% weighted pident, 100% qcov on 9/17 refs), so the block is not gross sequence loss. Neither the paper nor this replication localized the exact oriT deletion boundaries, tested the plasmid alone (cured of the 254 kb + 190 kb co-residents), nor examined T4SS expression. This is the single most epidemiologically load-bearing question in the paper (a non-conjugative mcr-1 plasmid would fundamentally reweight One-Health transmission risk).
next_steps: (1) Multiple sequence alignment of pEc45-2020-33kb vs the 9 transferable IncX4 refs restricted to the 200-500 bp typical oriT window immediately upstream of taxC/relaxase to localize the exact deletion/mutation; use oriTfinder + MEME + a hand-curated oriT motif library rather than oriTfinder alone (which the authors already ran and got null). (2) Attempt plasmid curing of Ec45-2020 to derive a 254kb-minus / 190kb-minus derivative and re-run conjugation from the derivative to test the 'conjugation competition' hypothesis directly. (3) RNA-seq of Ec45-2020 vs a known transferable IncX4/mcr-1 strain under log-phase conjugation conditions to test T4SS expression differences. (4) Electrotransform pEc45-2020-33kb into a naive E. coli K-12 background and re-test transferability to separate plasmid-intrinsic from strain-background effects. (5) If (1) does localize an oriT lesion, synthesize the ancestral oriT and knock it in — the strongest single experiment.

q: Is the paper's central 'cgMLST clusters the Hungarian duck ST162 with Chinese human ST162 strains but not the Chinese duck ST162' finding robust to (a) the specific 238-genome subsample chosen, (b) the K-12 MG1655 reference used to define the 2138 core genes vs a duck-adapted APEC reference, and (c) the Ridom SeqSphere+ v9.08 default allele-calling thresholds — none of which we could rerun in this replication?
basis: Claim C10 in our claims table was declared out-of-scope for the 15-minute rerun because it needs ~500 assemblies + Ridom SeqSphere+ (proprietary, not free-endpoint). The paper's core epidemiological punchline (that mcr-1 is moving human→duck rather than duck→human in this ST162 lineage) rests entirely on this single tree with no bootstrap/jackknife shown, no independent-scheme cross-check (e.g. chewBBACA + Enterobase cgMLST), and no time-calibrated analysis. Independent replication attempts on cgMLST trees in E. coli routinely show cluster boundaries move with reference choice and allele-caller parameters. This is a genuine unresolved question the paper's evidence cannot yet answer.
next_steps: (1) Reharvest the ~504 BV-BRC mcr-1 E. coli genomes cited in the paper via BV-BRC public API, re-run cgMLST with the open-source chewBBACA + EnteroBase E. coli cgMLST v1 scheme (2513 loci) on uicgpu, and compute the equivalent tree with GrapeTree. (2) Bootstrap (100x with genome subsampling) to quantify branch support around the ST162 Hungarian-duck / Chinese-human sister relationship. (3) Repeat with an APEC O1:K1:H7 reference (e.g. APEC_O1 CP000468) instead of K-12 to test reference-dependence. (4) If the sister relationship holds, add a time-calibrated Bayesian phylogeny (BEAST or BactDating) using isolation dates to test the human→duck direction claim. (5) Deposit the reanalysis in a Zenodo record so the tree is finally reproducible outside a proprietary tool.

q: The blaTEM-135–sul2–tet(A),(M) cassette is present in DUPLICATE on two different plasmids (CP134087 190 kb IncF hybrid and CP134088 254 kb IncH MDR) in the same cell — what is the mechanism (transposition, homologous recombination, IS-mediated capture) and evolutionary timing (pre-existing intracellular duplication vs recent independent acquisitions from a shared donor) of this duplication, and does the duplication increase the effective copy number / expression / stability of the AMR phenotype?
basis: The paper reports the duplication as a bare fact ('the gene cluster ... was identified in duplicate within the Ec45-2020 genome') and does not investigate the mechanism, the flanking IS/transposon architecture, whether the two copies are sequence-identical or diverged, or the phenotypic consequence. Our AMRFinderPlus rerun (report/evidence/amrfinder_full.tsv) confirms the duplication is genuine and both copies are 100% identity to reference — but with two 100%-identical copies AMRFinderPlus alone cannot distinguish very-recent duplication from independent acquisition, and our replication did not extract IS/Tn context.
next_steps: (1) Extract ±10 kb of flanking sequence around each of the two blaTEM-135-sul2-tet cassettes from CP134087 and CP134088 and align to identify shared IS elements (IS26, IS4321, Tn3 family are prime candidates), direct repeats (target-site duplications), and to determine if the boundaries are transposon-typical. (2) MLST of the two cassettes at the nucleotide level — if they are 100% identical over the flanking IS as well as the ORFs, the duplication is very recent (within-strain event). (3) qPCR of blaTEM-135 vs a chromosomal single-copy reference in Ec45-2020 to measure effective copy number and, paired with an isogenic single-copy transconjugant, MIC assays to test whether duplication raises ampicillin MIC. (4) Search BV-BRC for other mcr-1 poultry E. coli with the same cassette on multiple plasmids to test whether this is a strain-specific event or a broader phenomenon.

q: The paper reports colistin MIC of exactly 8 µg/mL for Ec45-2020 (right at the EUCAST resistance breakpoint), yet mcr-1.1 alleles typically confer MIC 4-16 µg/mL — is the modest MIC due to (a) low mcr-1 expression from the IncX4 promoter in the duck-derived strain background, (b) a compensating chromosomal mgrB/phoP/pmrAB polymorphism, or (c) fitness cost of the two large co-resident plasmids suppressing overall protein output — and does this modest MIC undermine the clinical significance of the isolate?
basis: The paper reports MIC 8 µg/mL without contextualizing it against typical mcr-1 MIC ranges or checking for chromosomal colistin-resistance-modifying mutations (mgrB truncations, phoP/pmrB gain-of-function). Our AMRFinderPlus rerun did not screen the chromosome specifically for the pmrAB/mgrB polymorphism panel because AMRFinderPlus's core-mutation module for E. coli colistin resistance is not comprehensive. The modest MIC is a real disconnect the paper leaves unaddressed and it affects the clinical/One-Health interpretation.
next_steps: (1) Extract the mgrB, phoP, phoQ, pmrA, pmrB coding + upstream 500 bp from CP134085 chromosome and align against the CLSI/EUCAST reference set of colistin-resistance-modifying variants. (2) RT-qPCR of mcr-1 transcript abundance in Ec45-2020 vs a known high-MIC (16-32 µg/mL) mcr-1 IncX4 reference under log-phase LB and under sub-MIC colistin induction. (3) Broth microdilution redo of the MIC in the deposited strain (available from BV-BRC-linked collections) using strict EUCAST ISO 20776 methodology to confirm 8 µg/mL is not a border-effect. (4) Attempt a plasmid-cured derivative and single-plasmid transconjugant to isolate the mcr-1 contribution from the other two large plasmids' background effect on MIC.

q: The 5 kb Col156 plasmid pEc45-2020-5kb (CP134090) and the 101 kb p0111 plasmid pEc45-2020-101kb (CP134086) are dismissed by the paper as carrying 'no AMR/VG determinants (data not shown)' — but Col plasmids commonly encode colicins (bacteriocin toxins) and mobilization functions that could plausibly contribute to (a) competitive fitness against gut competitors, (b) horizontal mobilization of other resident plasmids in trans, or (c) an unrecognized virulence contribution — and neither the paper nor our replication actually annotated their gene content, so their true role in the strain is completely unknown.
basis: Our AMRFinderPlus rerun confirmed 0 AMR/VF hits on both CP134086 and CP134090 (matching the paper), BUT AMRFinderPlus does not annotate colicins, mobilization genes, or general ORFs — it only calls curated AMR/VF panels. So 'no hits from AMRFinderPlus' is a much weaker claim than 'no biologically meaningful genes'. The p0111 replicon family in particular has been repeatedly implicated in APEC virulence in the literature, and Col156 plasmids frequently carry colicin E-family bacteriocins that shape gut community dynamics — none of which was tested. This is an evidence-strength gap in both the original paper and this replication.
next_steps: (1) Run Prokka + Bakta on CP134086 and CP134090 to get a full ORF annotation, then screen the ORF set against colicin V/E/M/B/K/Ia HMM libraries (Pfam PF03515, PF03526 etc.) and against the mobileOG database. (2) Compare the p0111 backbone against published p0111 APEC virulence plasmids (e.g. NC_007675) to determine whether pEc45-2020-101kb is a canonical APEC virulence plasmid missed by AMRFinderPlus/VFDB, or a stripped-down replicon-only skeleton. (3) If colicin ORFs are found on CP134090, functionally test bacteriocin activity via spot assays against a panel of commensal E. coli — colicin production could be the 'hidden' selective advantage keeping the 5 kb plasmid in the strain despite offering no antibiotic resistance. (4) Update the paper's Table S2 with a full gene inventory of these two plasmids (currently 'data not shown' — the classic red flag).
